turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you, Dr. Smith. Well, I suppose I’m here because for months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. And you know, as an office supervisor, I know a pattern when I see one. I manage a whole team of administrative staff, and I always tell them that details matter. Like this one girl we had, Brenda, she kept misfiling the invoices and blaming the new software, but I knew she was just spending half her day online shopping. She bought these awful, chunky neon heels... just completely inappropriate for a professional environment. But anyway. 

The pattern I'm talking about now is... well, my sister’s appointments keep getting moved around without my permission, and bills are showing up completely wrong. And then people just "forget" to call me back. Like the phone company—I was on hold for forty-five minutes on Tuesday, listening to that terrible elevator music, the one with the cheap saxophone, and then it just disconnected. But it's not just bad service. Even when everyone around me says it’s just mistakes or coincidences, I know what's really going on. I know they’re deliberately keeping information from me and trying to push me out of decisions.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that people are deliberately keeping information from them and pushing them out of decisions, despite others providing contradictory evidence that these are just mistakes.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned feeling like people are deliberately working against you; do you believe there is a specific group or organization actively conspiring to harm or discredit you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it’s not like it’s some... secret society in dark robes or anything silly like that. It’s the administration. The billing departments, the clinic schedulers, the office managers—they are all in on it together. Like I was saying, I’ve been seeing this exact same pattern for months now. My sister’s appointments get moved without a word, the bills show up completely wrong, and these people conveniently "forget" to call me back. 

And they all cover for each other! They’ll tell me, "Oh, it’s just a clerical error, ma'am." A clerical error! Please. I know a thing or two about clerical errors. When I took over my current department back in '98—or wait, was it '99? No, it was '98, because that was the year I went to Cabo and got that absolutely terrible sunburn on my shoulders. I couldn't even wear a normal bra for a week, I had to wear those awful sports ones. I hate those, they just flatten everything out and make you look like a box, you know? I had to wear button-down shirts the whole trip. 

But anyway, in my office, we didn't have "clerical errors" because I oversaw the filing system personally. We used color-coded tabs. Red for urgent, blue for pending. It’s not hard if you actually care about your job. But these people handling my sister's affairs? They aren't just making mistakes. Even when everyone else around me—my family, the staff—says it’s just coincidences or computer glitches, I know better. I know they are deliberately keeping information from me. They are trying to push me out of the decisions so they can just do whatever they want with her.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever heard any voices or sounds that other people around you couldn't hear?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? Oh, heavens no. I don't hear anything that isn't actually there. My hearing is perfectly normal. 

Well, I do get a little ringing in my left ear sometimes, but that's just because my niece dragged me to this awful indoor concert last summer. Some indie rock band, I don't even remember the name, but the acoustics in that venue were just dreadful. And the floors! So sticky. I really don't understand why places can't just mop properly. At the office, I make sure the night crew uses this heavy-duty citrus cleaner, because if you don't stay on top of it, the breakroom floor gets completely disgusting. 

Just last month, David—he's one of the junior accountants—dropped an entire Tupperware of leftover lasagna right in front of the refrigerator. Tomato sauce everywhere, all over the baseboards. And did he clean it up? Of course not. He just stood there looking at it like it was going to magically evaporate until I had to page the janitorial staff myself. Honestly, if I didn't oversee every little detail, that whole office would just fall apart in a week. Nobody takes pride in their environment anymore. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right. No, no voices or strange sounds. Just the usual ringing if it's too quiet.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or sounds that aren't there, stating her hearing is normal and she only experiences occasional ringing.

turns.doctor_question: Do you feel that you have to be constantly on guard because people in general—not just these specific administrators—are likely to use information against you if you're not careful?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, not people in general. Like I said, I'm not some crazy person who thinks the whole world is out to get me. I trust my team at work, mostly. Well, except for David, but that's just because he's incompetent, not malicious. I don't walk around thinking my neighbors or the mailman are trying to sabotage me. 

Speaking of the mail, did I tell you about the new carrier we have? He's just awful. He leaves the packages right on the edge of the porch where anyone driving by can see them. The old carrier, Mr. Henderson, he used to tuck them right behind the potted ferns. He was wonderful. He retired last spring, moved down to Florida. Naples, I think. Or maybe Sarasota. My aunt lived in Sarasota for a while. She had this beautiful little condo right on the water, but the humidity was just terrible for her hair. She had this very fine, thin hair, and the moment she stepped outside, it just went completely flat. She tried every product under the sun—mousses, gels, hairsprays that smelled like pure alcohol—but nothing worked. 

But anyway, no, I don't feel like I have to be on guard with everyone. It's just the clinic administration. They're the ones who are actively trying to mess with my sister's care. Everyone else is fine.

turns.doctor_question: Has your need for everything to be perfectly organized and your focus on following strict rules always been a part of who you are, even before these issues with your sister's care began?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yes, I suppose I've always liked things done a certain way. Organization is just common sense, isn't it? If you don't have a system, things just fall into absolute chaos. I've always been the one to keep things running smoothly, even back when I was in college. I shared an apartment with this girl, Sarah—oh, she was a sweetheart, but completely disorganized. She would leave her textbooks all over the dining table, and her coffee mugs... don't get me started on the coffee mugs. She had this terrible habit of leaving a little sip of coffee in the bottom of every mug and just leaving them on her nightstand. I had to go in there once a week and gather them up before they started growing mold. 

She ended up moving to Chicago after graduation. Or was it Detroit? Somewhere cold. I could never live anywhere that cold. The winters just dry out my skin terribly. I have to use this special lotion I order online, it has shea butter and some kind of almond oil in it. It smells wonderful, like a bakery, but not too sweet, you know? The shipping takes forever, though. They use this dreadful delivery service that always leaves the box out in the rain if I'm not home. Which reminds me of that terrible mail carrier we have now, I really need to call the post office about him. 

But, yes, to answer your question, I've always been organized. It's just who I am. It has nothing to do with what those administrators are doing to my sister, if that's what you're getting at. They're the ones breaking the rules, not me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that administrators are doing something to her sister and breaking rules.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, wandering from the topic of organization to a former roommate, cold weather, skin lotion, and a mail carrier before returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: If you were presented with clear, objective evidence that the administrators' actions were indeed just clerical errors and not a deliberate attempt to target you, would you be able to accept that explanation?
turns.patient_response:
Objective evidence? Well, what would that even look like? Because everyone already says it’s just mistakes. They love that word. 'Oh, it's just a clerical error, we're so sorry.' But I’m here because for months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. My sister’s appointments magically get moved without my authorization, the billing statements show up completely wrong, and people conveniently 'forget' to call me back. 

Which, speaking of forgetting to call back, is exactly the excuse people used when we switched to that new VoIP phone system at the office last fall. Total disaster. The sales rep—this young guy wearing a suit that was entirely too tight, you know the style the young men wear now with the ankles showing? It looks ridiculous, especially in a professional setting. You'd think they'd want to look like adults. Anyway, he promised us this completely seamless call routing, but for the first three weeks, half the calls from our vendors were going straight to a phantom voicemail box that nobody even had the password to. I had to spend four hours on hold with their tech support, listening to this awful elevator music. It was a synthesized version of 'The Girl from Ipanema' on an endless loop. I still hear it in my nightmares. I finally had to threaten to cancel the entire contract before they sent someone out to fix it. 

But no, to answer your question, I wouldn't accept that explanation from the clinic. I've been an office supervisor for almost thirty years. I know what a simple filing error looks like, and I know what a coordinated effort looks like. Even when everyone there smiles and says it’s just mistakes, I know the truth. I know they’re deliberately keeping information from me and trying to push me out of the decisions regarding my sister's care. You don't just 'accidentally' do all of that month after month.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly states they would not accept objective evidence to the contrary, maintaining a fixed belief that the clinic is deliberately targeting them and keeping information from them.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality by drifting into a long, unrelated story about a VoIP phone system, a sales rep's suit, and hold music before eventually returning to answer the doctor's question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever been told by colleagues or family members that your focus on order and your high standards for others have caused significant problems or conflicts in your relationships or at work?
turns.patient_response:
Problems? No, I wouldn't say that. People appreciate my standards, really. I mean, if you don't have high standards in an office setting, things just fall apart. Nobody has ever come up to me and said I’m causing conflicts just because I expect people to do their jobs correctly. 

Take our quarterly reports, for example. I always insist we use the heavy-weight paper for the final printouts. It just looks more professional. I have to order it special from this supplier in Ohio because the local places only carry that flimsy 20-pound stock. It’s terrible paper, really. If you use a gel pen on it, it bleeds right through to the other side. I love a good gel pen, though. I found these wonderful navy blue ones at a little stationery shop when I was visiting my niece in Seattle last year. 

Oh, Seattle is beautiful, but it rained almost the entire time we were there. We went to that famous market, you know the one where they throw the fish? It’s completely unsanitary if you ask me, just tossing raw salmon over people's heads. My niece thought it was hilarious, but she’s always had a strange sense of humor. She’s studying graphic design, which I suppose explains it. She designed her own wedding invitations and they didn't even use capital letters. Just all lowercase. I asked her if her computer's shift key was broken! She didn't think that was very funny. They had a lovely reception, though. The catering was done by this little Italian place—the chicken piccata was to die for, but the capers were a bit too salty. 

But anyway, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my colleagues. No, nobody has told me my focus on order is a problem. They know I run a tight ship, and they respect that. It's certainly not causing any big issues with my family or at work.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from office standards to paper, pens, a trip to Seattle, a fish market, and a wedding before forgetting the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever lost a job, had a team member resign, or experienced a significant falling out with a close friend or family member specifically because they felt you were being too demanding or inflexible with your rules?
turns.patient_response:
Lost a job? Heavens, no. I’m still managing all my responsibilities perfectly well, just like I always have. Though... I suppose I will admit I've had a few uncomfortable conversations at work lately. I’ve just been pressing people a bit harder than I used to about their routine mistakes. 

Like Susan in accounts payable. She keeps forgetting to date the invoices. It's not a difficult task, there's a stamp right on her desk. A self-inking one. I bought it for her myself at that little office supply store on 4th Street before it closed down. It’s such a shame they closed, they had the absolute best selection of Manila folders. The ones with the reinforced tabs. Now everything you buy online is so flimsy. I ordered some curtains online last month for my living room, supposedly they were blackout curtains, but they let the streetlights right in. The streetlights in my neighborhood are those new LED ones, terribly bright, they give everything this harsh blue tint at night. It completely washes out my hydrangeas in the front yard. I spend hours on those hydrangeas, making sure the soil pH is just right so they stay that vibrant purple. I use a special fertilizer I get from... 

Wait, what was the rest of your question? Oh, family. Right. Well, no one has stopped speaking to me or anything dramatic like that, but our family meetings have definitely become tense. I can tell it has started to affect how people respond to me when we get together. My brother-in-law gets this tight look on his face whenever I try to go over the care schedule. He’s always been a bit touchy, though. He’s a Leo, you know. I don’t put too much stock in astrology, but my goodness, he fits the description. Always has to be the center of attention. He wore a bright red sweater to my mother's funeral! Who wears red to a funeral? It was cashmere, at least, but still. I prefer a nice subtle navy or charcoal grey. Grey is just so much more versatile, don't you think? You can pair it with silver jewelry, or gold if it's a warmer grey...

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits marked tangentiality, repeatedly drifting from the original topic into long, unrelated tangents about office supplies, curtains, streetlights, hydrangeas, and astrology.

turns.patient_response:
All-consuming? Heavens, no. Outside of dealing with my sister’s appointments and trying to get straight answers out of those people, I still keep my home in perfect order, I pay my bills, and I do my job.

I was looking for crushed tomatoes for my chili—I use a dash of cinnamon in it, it’s a secret ingredient I learned from a cooking show years ago. turns.doctor_question: Do you feel that you are generally a more suspicious or skeptical person than most people you know, even in situations unrelated to your sister's care?
turns.patient_response:
Suspicious? Me? No, I wouldn't say that at all. I think I'm just naturally observant. There's a very big difference between being suspicious and just having your eyes open to the world. 

Most people just walk around completely oblivious to their surroundings. Like... well, just yesterday at the dry cleaners. I've been going to Mr. Chen's on Elm Street for fifteen years. He always does a wonderful sharp crease on my slacks. But I noticed right away that the smell in the shop was different when I walked in. They changed their cleaning solvent. I asked his daughter about it—she works the register on Tuesdays and Thursdays because she's taking classes at the community college. Dental hygiene, I think. Which is a very sensible career, really. People will always need their teeth cleaned. My own dentist, Dr. Aris, has this beautiful saltwater aquarium in his waiting room. It’s so soothing to watch the little neon tetras darting around in the coral. I used to have a goldfish when I was a little girl, won him at the county fair by throwing a ping-pong ball into a little glass bowl. We named him Barnaby... wait, no, Barnaby is my neighbor's dog, the golden retriever I told you about. We named the fish... oh, what was it? Captain something. Captain Crunch? No, that's the cereal. My brother used to eat that every single morning, drove my mother crazy with the crunching noises. 

But... oh dear, I've lost my train of thought. What were you asking me? Oh, right, about being skeptical. No, I trust people just fine in my day-to-day life. I just pay attention to the details that other people completely ignore.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and derailment, wandering from dry cleaners to dental hygiene, aquariums, and childhood pets before losing her train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over the last several years, have you ever felt that close friends or business partners were acting behind your back to betray your trust, even when there was no clear evidence to suggest it?
turns.patient_response:
Betray my trust? Goodness, no. I don't have any reason to think my friends or coworkers are doing anything behind my back. My friends are very dear to me, we're completely honest with one another. 

My friend Barbara, for instance, we've been doing a Tuesday night book club for nearly a decade. Though, to be perfectly honest, it's less about the books lately and more about the wine and cheese. Barbara always brings this incredible baked brie with fig jam. She gets the jam from a little specialty shop downtown. Parking down there is just a nightmare, though. Have you been down there lately? They put in those new electronic meters where you have to type in your license plate number, and half the time the screen is so glaring from the sun you can't even read what you're typing. 

I got a parking ticket last month because the machine didn't register the 'Q' in my license plate properly. Thirty-five dollars! I tried to appeal it, but the city office is only open from 10 AM to 2 PM on weekdays. Who has time for that when they work full time? I oversee a staff of fourteen people at the office, I can't just take a two-hour lunch to go argue with the parking authority. Especially not now. We've got our quarterly reports due, and the new software the company just installed keeps freezing whenever we try to export the spreadsheets. It's supposed to be this new cloud-based system that makes everything faster, but I spend half my morning just waiting for the little loading wheel to stop spinning on my screen. 

But... oh dear, I'm rambling about the office again. What was it you just asked me? Did you ask if Barbara liked the book this week? Because I honestly don't think she even read the first chapter.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits marked tangentiality, drifting from the topic of her friends to cheese, parking meters, and office software, ultimately forgetting the doctor's original question.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having any reason to believe that friends or coworkers are acting behind her back or betraying her trust.

turns.doctor_question: Setting aside this situation with the clinic, have you ever felt that you needed to be extremely guarded or secretive with friends or colleagues because you were worried they might use information against you?
turns.patient_response:
Guarded with my friends? Oh, no, not at all. I’m an open book with the people I care about. I don’t have any reason to think they’d use anything against me. My colleagues and I get along just fine, too. 

Although, speaking of the office, I did have to have a very firm word with the cleaning staff last week. They’ve started using this lemon-scented polish on the conference room table, and it leaves the most awful streaks. I told them, you really just need a microfiber cloth and a tiny bit of water. It’s real wood veneer, you know. You can’t just spray chemicals all over it. My grandmother had this beautiful antique mahogany dining table—claw feet, the whole nine yards. She used to rub it down with beeswax once a month. It smelled wonderful, like honey and old paper. She kept all her important documents in this little cedar chest under the stairs. Birth certificates, old love letters from my grandfather when he was stationed in Germany... 

He brought her back this incredible cuckoo clock from the Black Forest. The little bird would pop out on the hour, but the mechanism got stuck when I was about twelve. My dad tried to fix it, took the whole back off, but he just ended up with a pile of gears on the kitchen counter. He was always doing that—taking things apart and never quite getting them back together. Like the lawnmower. We had to hire the neighbor boy to cut the grass for an entire summer because dad insisted he was going to rebuild the carburetor. 

But... oh, goodness, I’m doing it again, aren’t I? Getting completely off track. What were we just talking about? Did you ask about my grandfather’s clock?

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech and derailment, drifting from office cleaning to a grandmother's table, a cuckoo clock, and a broken lawnmower, completely losing track of the original question.

turns.doctor_question: When you are not dealing with the situation at the clinic, do you find yourself feeling a strong, internal need to organize your daily activities or personal environment into strict, rigid systems, even when no one else is watching?
turns.patient_response:
Strict, rigid systems? No, I wouldn't say that. I like things to be tidy, of course, but I don't have any sort of rigid system at home. I just put things where they belong. 

Like my spices, for instance. I keep them in a little rack next to the stove, but I don't alphabetize them or anything silly like that. Though I did have to throw out my paprika last week because it had completely lost its color. It looked like dust! You really have to be careful with spices, they lose their potency so quickly. I was trying to make my mother's beef stew recipe. She always used a pinch of smoked paprika right at the end. It gave it this wonderful depth. She used to make it every Sunday during the winter. We'd eat it in the living room while watching the Sunday night movie on television. Back when there were only three channels and you actually had to get up from the couch to change them! The dial on our old Zenith TV was so stiff, I used to have to use both hands to turn it. 

We watched the Wizard of Oz on that TV every year when they broadcast it. I was always so terrified of those flying monkeys. Still am, if I'm being honest. I saw a documentary about how they made the costumes for that movie, and it was fascinating. They used real monkey fur, which is just awful to think about now, isn't it? The things people used to do before they knew better. Like asbestos in the ceilings. My old elementary school had to be completely closed down for a year to remove all the asbestos. 

But... oh, I've wandered off again, haven't I? I'm so sorry. What was your question? Did you ask if I like to cook?

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality and derailment, wandering from the topic of spices to an old TV, a movie, monkey fur, and asbestos, eventually forgetting the original question.

turns.doctor_question: When you observe someone else failing to follow a rule or failing to meet your standards, do you find yourself feeling that they are intentionally doing it to undermine or disrespect you, rather than simply being careless or incompetent?
turns.patient_response:
Undermine me? Oh, no. No, I don't think that at all. When people mess up, it's usually just because they aren't paying attention. Or they're just... well, not very good at what they do. Like the new girl at the office, Sarah. She's sweet, but she couldn't organize a two-car parade. 

She keeps putting the incoming mail in the outgoing tray. I've showed her three times, and she just smiles and nods, and then the next day, there's the mail, sitting in the wrong tray. It's just carelessness, really. Young people today, they're so distracted by their phones. She's always tapping away on that screen. My niece is the same way. We went to lunch last weekend at this lovely little bistro on 4th Street—the one with the blue awnings? They do a fantastic quiche lorraine. But my niece spent the entire meal taking pictures of her food. I said to her, "Honey, it's going to get cold," but she just had to get the lighting right for her... what do they call it? Instagram? 

I don't understand it, honestly. Why do strangers on the internet care what you're eating for lunch? I tried to set up a Facebook account once, just to see pictures of my cousin's new baby, but the password requirements were ridiculous. It had to have a capital letter, a number, a special character, and be at least twelve characters long. By the time I came up with something that worked, I'd forgotten what it was! I wrote it down on a sticky note, but then the note fell off my monitor and the vacuum cleaner got it. 

I have a terrible time with vacuums. The belts always snap on me. I bought one of those expensive bagless ones last year, thinking it would be easier, but emptying the canister is just a nightmare. The dust goes everywhere. You end up having to vacuum again just to clean up from emptying the vacuum! 

But... wait. I'm sorry, I've completely lost the thread again. What were we talking about? Did you ask about the mail at the office?

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits highly tangential speech, drifting from a coworker to her niece, social media, passwords, and vacuum cleaners, before completely losing the original topic of conversation.
